label: Psychology
title: Why Endings Matter More Than You Think – The Peak-End Rule
description: Why would anyone choose more pain over less? In this calm video essay we look at Daniel Kahneman's cold-water experiment, the colonoscopy studies with Donald Redelmeier, and the peak-end rule: our memory of an experience is shaped mostly by its most intense moment and by how it ends, while its length barely counts. We explore the difference between the experiencing self and the remembering self – and what this means for how we design our days, our holidays and our goodbyes.

sections.text:
Imagine you could choose between two painful experiences. The first one lasts sixty seconds. The second one is exactly the same, but it lasts ninety seconds.

Which would you choose to repeat? The answer seems obvious. Less pain is better than more pain.

And yet, in a now famous experiment, most people chose the longer one.

They were not confused, and they were not careless. They were following a quiet rule that shapes almost every memory we have. Once you see it, you start to notice it everywhere: in holidays, in relationships, in the way you remember your own life.

sections.heading: The Cold Water Experiment
sections.text:
In 1993, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman and his colleagues asked volunteers to hold one hand in cold water, at around fourteen degrees Celsius. Cold enough to be clearly unpleasant.

Each person went through two trials. In the short trial, the hand stayed in the cold water for sixty seconds. In the long trial, it stayed in for the same sixty seconds at the same temperature, and then for thirty seconds more. During those extra thirty seconds, warmer water was let in, so the temperature rose by about one degree. Still cold, still unpleasant, but a little less so.

Objectively, the long trial contained everything the short trial did, plus extra discomfort.

Then came the choice. Which trial would they rather repeat? About two thirds of the participants chose the long one.

Why? Because the long trial ended better. And when we look back, the ending weighs far more than the minutes that came before.

sections.heading: Peaks, Endings and Missing Time
sections.text:
Kahneman and his colleagues called this the peak-end rule. When we remember an experience, we do not add up every moment. Instead, our judgment is shaped mostly by two points: the most intense moment, the peak, and the final moment, the end.

One rough way to picture it: memory behaves as if it takes something close to the average of the peak and the end, and quietly drops the rest. It is not an exact formula, and later research has found many exceptions. But as a pattern, it has proven remarkably robust.

The second part of the finding is just as strange. They called it duration neglect. How long an experience lasted has surprisingly little effect on how good or bad we remember it to be. Twice as long does not feel twice as bad in memory. Often it barely registers at all.

In a related study, Barbara Fredrickson and Kahneman showed people short film clips, some pleasant, some unpleasant, and of different lengths. When people later rated the clips as a whole, the length of the clip made little difference.

Our memory, it seems, works less like a recording and more like a few snapshots. And the last snapshot is usually the one we keep.

sections.heading: What Happened in the Hospital
sections.text:
This could sound like a laboratory curiosity. But the same pattern appeared in a much more serious setting.

In a study published in 1996, the physician Donald Redelmeier and Kahneman followed patients undergoing colonoscopy, which at the time was often done without full sedation and could be quite painful. Every sixty seconds during the procedure, patients rated their pain on a scale from zero to ten. Afterwards, they gave an overall judgment of how bad it had been.

The length of the procedure varied widely, from a few minutes to more than an hour. But it hardly predicted how patients remembered it. What mattered most was the worst moment, and the last few minutes.

So a patient whose procedure was short but ended at a painful peak could remember it as worse than a patient whose procedure was much longer, with more pain in total, but ended gently.

In a later randomised trial, Redelmeier, Joel Katz and Kahneman tested this directly. For some patients, the end of the procedure was extended by a short, milder period. Those patients remembered the whole procedure as less unpleasant, and they were somewhat more likely to return for a follow-up examination.

sections.heading: Two Selves

quote.lead: Long before any of these studies, Shakespeare gave a play a title that has become a proverb. In the play, its heroine Helena puts it this way:
quote.text: All's well that ends well; still the fine's the crown; whate'er the course, the end is the renown.
quote.author: William Shakespeare, All's Well That Ends Well, Act IV, Scene 4

sections.text:
Kahneman later described this in terms of two selves.

The experiencing self lives in the present. It is the one that feels the cold water, minute by minute. It asks: how does this feel right now?

The remembering self is the one that looks back. It tells the story, keeps score, and makes the decisions about what to do next time. It asks: how was it, all in all?

The two do not always agree. And here is the uncomfortable part: it is mostly the remembering self that chooses. It chose the longer cold-water trial, even though the experiencing self would have suffered more.

You can see the same tension in everyday life. A long, pleasant holiday with a stressful final day can be remembered as disappointing. A difficult week that ends with a good evening among friends can be remembered as fine.

This does not make memory a liar. It simply has its own way of keeping accounts. The fine, as Shakespeare put it, is the crown.

sections.heading: Designing Better Endings
sections.text:
If endings carry so much weight, we can use that gently and honestly.

On a holiday, you might save something good for the last day, instead of spending it packing in a rush. The final evening often becomes the frame for the whole trip.

In a hard conversation, you can take a moment at the end to say something warm and true. Not to hide the difficulty, but so it does not end on its sharpest point.

At the end of a working day, you might close with a small task you can finish, rather than stopping in the middle of a problem.

And with the people you love, goodbyes are worth a little care. A kind word at the door is a small thing. In memory, it may count for more than you think.

But there is a caution here too. The remembering self is not the whole of life. A good ending does not undo long stretches of real difficulty for the one living through them. The minutes matter, even if memory forgets them.

sections.heading: The Story We Keep
sections.text:
We live our lives moment by moment, but we keep them as stories. And stories are shaped by their high points and their endings.

That is worth knowing, both as a warning and as an invitation. A warning, because our memories can mislead us about what was really good for us. An invitation, because even after a difficult stretch, the next moment can still change how the story is told.

Perhaps the kindest thing we can do with this knowledge is to remember that the people around us carry their own stories too. The way we end our time with them becomes part of how they remember it.

The ending is not yet written. And it seems to count for a great deal.

short.title: Why people chose more pain over less
short.hook: They chose the longer pain. Why?
short.text:
In 1993, volunteers held one hand in cold water. Once for sixty seconds. Once for ninety: the same sixty seconds, plus thirty more as the water got slightly warmer.

Then they chose which trial to repeat. About two thirds chose the longer one.

Daniel Kahneman called this the peak-end rule. Our memory of an experience is shaped mostly by its most intense moment and by how it ends. How long it lasted barely counts.

So if endings matter this much, give them a little care. A kind word at the door may count for more than you think.
